scenario: A Friday fix deployed from a developer's laptop included an uncommitted change and took checkout down for two hours. Nobody could tell what had been deployed.
stem: Which rule most directly prevents a repeat?
options: Only senior developers may deploy from their laptops
The pipeline is the only way to production, and engineers hold read-only access to production except through an emergency process
Deployments are banned on Fridays
Every developer keeps a deployment log in a spreadsheet
explanation: A pipeline deploys only committed, built and tested code and records exactly what ran and when. Seniority, calendars and manual logs all still allow unrecorded, unreviewed changes from a laptop.

stem: What distinguishes continuous delivery from continuous deployment?
options: Continuous delivery skips testing
Continuous delivery keeps every passing change deployable at the push of a button; continuous deployment ships every passing change to production automatically
Continuous deployment is only for containers
They are different names for continuous integration
explanation: Both depend on continuous integration producing a tested artefact. The difference is the final step: a human decision, or none. Many teams use continuous delivery with an approval for production.

scenario: Leadership proposes hiring a 'DevOps team' to own all pipelines, so developers can focus on features.
options: DevOps engineers are expensive
It creates a new silo between building and running software, which is the problem DevOps exists to remove
Pipelines cannot be shared
Azure does not support dedicated DevOps teams
explanation: DevOps is a way of working in which the people who build software also ship and run it. A central team can provide platforms and templates, but if it owns every pipeline, developers lose sight of production and hand-offs return.

scenario: The API's code is in Azure DevOps, the mobile app in GitHub, and the team prefers GitHub. An on-premises deployment runs reliably in Azure Pipelines.
stem: What is the most pragmatic plan?
options: Move everything, including work item history and the on-premises pipeline, to GitHub this quarter
Move everything back into Azure DevOps
Consolidate application code and CI/CD on GitHub, keep the working Azure Pipeline and Boards for now, and give each tool a clear job
Keep two copies of every repository, one in each
explanation: Start where the code and the team already are, and migrate only when running both costs more than moving. A working pipeline and a business backlog can stay put with clear boundaries. Duplicate repositories are the worst of both.

scenario: The pipeline deploys the API, but engineers still change App Service settings in the portal during incidents. The next deployment keeps reverting their fixes.
options: The pipeline is too slow
The pipeline is not the only way in, so the portal and the code disagree; changes belong in code and flow through the pipeline
Portal changes are always overwritten by Azure
App Service does not support settings
explanation: When portal edits continue alongside a pipeline, environments drift and deployments undo unrecorded fixes. Defining configuration as code and making the pipeline the single path keeps them consistent.

stem: Which Azure DevOps service would host a private npm package shared by several of the shop's services?
options: Azure Boards
Azure Test Plans
Azure Artifacts
Azure Repos
explanation: Azure Artifacts provides private package feeds for npm, NuGet, Maven and Python. Boards tracks work, Test Plans manages testing, and Repos stores Git repositories.

stem: Which practice closes the DevOps loop?
options: Deploying more often regardless of outcomes
Feeding production signals - SLOs, alerts, incidents - back into the backlog so they shape the next changes
Writing longer release notes
Adding more approval steps
explanation: Speed without feedback just breaks things faster. Monitoring and incident learnings turned into work items are what make the next change better informed.

stem: Which combination is a supported, sensible mix?
options: Azure Boards work items linked to pull requests in GitHub repositories
Two copies of each repository kept in sync by hand
Separate backlogs in both tools for the same product
Deploying half the environments from each tool with different artefacts
explanation: Azure Boards integrates with GitHub, so planning can stay in Boards while code lives on GitHub. The other options duplicate sources of truth or build artefacts differently per environment, which undermines repeatability.
